source.title: The efficacy of dapagliflozin combined with hypoglycaemic drugs in treating type 2 diabetes mellitus: meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials

atoms.canonical_statement: The review evaluated the efficacy of dapagliflozin versus placebo when added to conventional antidiabetic drugs, focusing on HbA1c, fasting plasma glucose, and body weight in adults with type 2 diabetes.
The authors conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis in accordance with PRISMA and prospectively registered the protocol in PROSPERO as CRD42013005034.

The literature search used MEDLINE via PubMed, EMBASE via OVID, the Cochrane Library, Google Scholar, ClinicalTrials.gov, Google, and manual journal searching; the initial search was July 9, 2013 and the last update was October 21, 2013.
Only randomized controlled trials were eligible; observational, cohort, case-control, case-series, and laboratory studies were excluded.

population.label: Randomized controlled trials in adults with type 2 diabetes
exclusion_criteria: Observational, cohort, case-control, case-series, and laboratory studies

population.label: Adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus

population.label: Add-on dapagliflozin trials

atoms.canonical_statement: Eligible comparators used placebo combined with the same conventional antidiabetic background drugs; placebo-only control trials were excluded.

population.label: Matched-background placebo-controlled trials
inclusion_criteria: Placebo plus corresponding conventional antidiabetic drugs

atoms.canonical_statement: Eligible trials had to report all three review outcomes: HbA1c, fasting plasma glucose, and body weight.

population.label: Trials reporting all required outcomes

atoms.canonical_statement: At least two reviewers evaluated studies for eligibility, and disagreements were resolved by discussion.
One reviewer extracted trial data and another reviewer verified the extraction.
The review assessed trial design, execution, and reporting with the Cochrane risk-of-bias tool and assessed outcome-level evidence quality using GRADE profiler 3.2.
Meta-analysis used R 3.0.1 with metafor and Review Manager 5.2; other statistical tests and regression analyses used R 3.0.1.
The primary meta-analyses used random-effects models to compare changes in HbA1c, fasting plasma glucose, and body weight between 10 mg dapagliflozin and placebo arms on matched background therapy.
Continuous outcomes were extracted as adjusted mean differences with 95% confidence intervals, and the pooled mean differences represented the mean of those adjusted mean differences.
The authors performed subgroup analyses by background drug and by follow-up duration of 24 weeks or less versus more than 24 weeks, and they also used meta-regression for follow-up duration.
Publication bias was assessed with funnel plots and Egger regression and adjusted with trim-and-fill.
Heterogeneity was evaluated with I-squared; the review defined values below 25% as low and values above 75% as high heterogeneity.
Sensitivity analyses excluded trials with high or unclear risk-of-bias concerns and separately excluded interim reports to retain endpoint results.
The principal efficacy comparison used dapagliflozin 10 mg as add-on therapy to conventional antidiabetic drugs.

population.label: Adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus in eligible randomized controlled trials

atoms.canonical_statement: The search assessed 380 citations: 231 from bibliographic databases and 149 from supplementary Google and Google Scholar searching.

Abstract screening excluded 139 non-randomized studies and seven pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic studies; eight of the remaining 20 randomized trials failed the intervention/comparator criteria, leaving 12 trials for quantitative synthesis.
The 12 included randomized trials evaluated add-on dapagliflozin doses of 2.5, 5, or 10 mg with metformin, insulin, glimepiride, pioglitazone, or metformin/sitagliptin in adults with type 2 diabetes.

population.label: Participants in 12 included randomized controlled trials

atoms.canonical_statement: Most included trials used last observation carried forward, and the extracted adjusted mean differences were based on ANCOVA models.
Four included randomized trials had more than one Cochrane risk-of-bias item rated unclear.
The common risk-of-bias concern was detection bias related to absent reporting of blinding.
The review rated the HbA1c evidence as high quality under GRADE.
The review rated the fasting-plasma-glucose evidence as high quality under GRADE.
The review rated the body-weight evidence as moderate quality under GRADE because of publication bias.

Across 12 randomized trials and 3,986 participants, add-on dapagliflozin reduced HbA1c by a pooled mean difference of 0.52 percentage points versus matched-background placebo (MD -0.52%; 95% CI -0.60 to -0.45; p<0.001).

atoms.canonical_statement: The authors concluded that dapagliflozin added to conventional antidiabetic drugs improved glycaemic control and reduced weight gain in type 2 diabetes, particularly when conventional drugs provided inadequate glycaemic control.
The authors considered the pooled HbA1c, fasting-plasma-glucose, and body-weight findings robust to their risk-of-bias and interim-report sensitivity analyses.
The authors stated that they planned to update the meta-analysis as additional randomized trials with proper registration and less potential bias became available.
Four included randomized trials had only short follow-up, limiting the review's ability to assess longer-term effects.
For consistency, the meta-analysis used only the 10 mg dapagliflozin dose even though included trials also studied 2.5 mg and 5 mg doses.
The small number of randomized trials could cause the meta-regression R-squared values to overestimate the associations with follow-up duration.
Most included trials used last observation carried forward and excluded post-rescue data; the authors noted this could overstate effects and underestimate standard errors and p values.
All eligible randomized trials were sponsored by Bristol-Myers Squibb or AstraZeneca, which the authors identified as a potential source of favorable-outcome bias.
The body-weight analysis showed statistically significant publication bias by Egger regression, and the review downgraded its GRADE quality to moderate.

atoms.canonical_statement: The University of Macau funded the work of Yu-nan Sun, Yi Zhou, and Siu-wai Leung through grant MYRG190-Y3-L3-ICMS11-LSW.
The authors reported no competing interests.
The article states that no additional data are available.

The abstract reverses the ordering of the two sensitivity-analysis result sets relative to the Results section: the abstract assigns -0.56/-1.11/-2.23 to exclusion of low-quality trials and -0.50/-1.08/-2.08 to exclusion of interim trials, whereas the Results section assigns them in the opposite way.
GRADE Table 2 labels the HbA1c evidence as 3,986 participants from 14 studies, while the narrative Results section states that the HbA1c analysis included 12 randomized trials.
GRADE Table 2 labels the body-weight evidence as 4,008 participants from 14 studies, while the narrative Results section states that the body-weight analysis included 12 randomized trials.

Table 3 prints a fasting-plasma-glucose week coefficient of -0.01 with a 95% confidence interval of 0.004 to 0.012, an interval that is incompatible in sign with the printed point estimate; the Results prose also describes -1.52 as the follow-up-duration coefficient although Table 3 presents -1.52 as the intercept.

The body-weight meta-regression is described as significant with R-squared 1 and p<0.01, while Table 3 prints a week estimate of -0.01 with 95% CI -0.02 to 0.01, which crosses zero; the source does not reconcile the difference.
